q: A program executes 2×10⁹ instructions with an average CPI of 1.5 on a 3 GHz processor. What is the CPU time?
explain: CPU time = (IC × CPI) / clock rate = (2×10⁹ × 1.5) / 3×10⁹ = 1.0 s.

q: A workload is 50% ALU (CPI 1), 30% loads (CPI 5), and 20% branches (CPI 2). Compute the weighted CPI.
explain: Multiply each class's CPI by its share of instructions and add.

q: Computer A runs a program in 20 s and computer B runs it in 40 s. How much faster is A?
explain: Speedup = Time_B / Time_A = 40/20 = 2.0. Times flip when converting to performance.

q: With 80% of a program parallelizable and 4 processors, Amdahl's law gives what speedup?
With P = 0.80, what is the maximum speedup with unlimited processors?
explain: As N → ∞, speedup → 1/(1−P) = 1/0.20 = 5×. The serial fraction is the ceiling.

q: CPU time and elapsed time mean the same thing.
explain: Elapsed time is wall-clock time including I/O, OS overhead, and idle time. CPU time counts only cycles spent on your program.

q: Which level of the memory hierarchy is managed to reduce memory latency and is built from SRAM?
explain: Caches (L1/L2/L3) sit between registers and DRAM, are built from SRAM, and are sized in KB to MB.

q: Why is MIPS a misleading performance metric?
answer: MIPS counts instructions per second, but instructions differ in complexity across ISAs, so one x86 instruction is not one RISC-V instruction. It also ignores CPI, so a machine can have high MIPS and still be slow. Execution time captures IC, CPI, and cycle time together.
explain: A program with more, simpler instructions can still finish sooner.

q: Branch prediction is an example of which of the seven great ideas?
explain: Prediction pre-fetches the likely next instruction to avoid pipeline stalls. It supports pipelining but is its own idea.

q: What is 101011₂ in decimal?
Convert 38₁₀ to binary.
explain: Divide by 2 and read remainders upward: 0,1,1,0,0,1 → 100110. Check: 32+4+2 = 38.

q: What is 1234₁₀ in hexadecimal?
Find the 8-bit two's complement of 01001010₂ and give its decimal value.
answer: Invert all bits: 10110101. Add 1: 10110110. The original is 74, so this represents −74. Check by adding: 01001010 + 10110110 = 1 00000000, and the low 8 bits are zero.
explain: Two's complement = invert + add 1.

q: What is the signed range of an 8-bit two's complement number?
explain: −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1. There is one more negative value than positive because zero occupies a positive slot.

q: Convert binary 1011011101 to hexadecimal.
explain: Pad on the left to 0010 1101 1101, then convert each group: 2, D, D → 0x2DD.

q: When converting binary to hex you group the bits in fours starting from the left.
explain: Group from the right and pad the left with zeros. Grouping from the left is the classic mistake.

q: 6A2₁₆ + 49A₁₆ = ?
explain: 2 + A = C; A + 9 = 19 → 3 carry 1; 1 + 6 + 4 = B. Result 0xB3C.

q: In 8 bits, adding 10110111 (183) + 01101110 (110) produces a carry out of the MSB. What is this called?
explain: 183 + 110 = 293 needs 9 bits. A carry out of the MSB is unsigned overflow; the stored result wraps to 37.

q: How wide is a base RISC-V instruction, and why does that matter?
choices: Fixed 32 bits, for simple uniform decode and efficient pipelining
Fixed 64 bits, to match the register width
explain: Fixed-length instructions are what make the decode logic simple and pipelining efficient.

q: What happens when a program writes to register x0?
choices: The write is discarded; reads always return 0
explain: x0 is hardwired zero: reads return 0 and writes are discarded. That is why beq x0, x0, Label is an unconditional branch.

q: Which registers must a called function save and restore if it uses them?
explain: s registers and sp are callee-saved. The a and t registers are caller-saved, so the caller protects them if needed.

q: Which instruction format does sw use, and why not I-type?
choices: R, because it has two sources
S, because it needs two source registers and no destination, so the immediate is split
I, because it has an immediate
B, because it computes an address
explain: A store needs rs1 (base) and rs2 (data) and no rd, so the 5 bits I-type would use for rd hold the low half of the immediate.

q: How many bits are the opcode, rd, rs1, rs2, funct3, and funct7 fields?
explain: 7 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 3 + 7 = 32 bits exactly, which is the R-type layout.

q: Decode 0x002082B3 into assembly, showing the fields.
answer: Binary: 0000000 00010 00001 000 00101 0110011. Opcode 0110011 = R-type ALU. funct3 000 with funct7 0000000 = ADD. rd = 00101 = x5, rs1 = 00001 = x1, rs2 = 00010 = x2. So the instruction is add x5, x1, x2.
explain: Read the opcode first to learn the format, then pull the fixed-position fields.

q: Which instruction loads a 32-bit word from memory?
explain: lw loads a word; lb loads a sign-extended byte; sw stores; lui loads an upper immediate.

q: In RISC-V, arithmetic instructions can operate directly on memory operands.
explain: RISC-V is a load/store architecture: arithmetic works only on registers, and memory is reached through loads and stores. Direct memory operands are a CISC (x86) feature.

q: Which bitwise operation clears selected bits while keeping the rest?
choices: AND with a mask that has 0s in those positions
OR with a mask that has 1s in those positions
explain: AND clears where the mask is 0. OR sets, XOR toggles.

q: x5 = 0x12345678. After and x6, x5, 0x000000FF, what is x6?
explain: The mask keeps only the lowest byte, 0x78.

q: Using only addi and shifts, build the mask 0xFFFFFF00 in x11 and explain each step.
answer: addi x11, x0, -1 puts 0xFFFFFFFF (all ones) in x11, because -1 sign-extends to all ones. Then slli x11, x11, 8 shifts left by 8, filling the low 8 bits with zeros, giving 0xFFFFFF00.
explain: The same trick with srli 16 builds 0x0000FFFF.

q: x5 = 0x12345678. Write instructions to extract the second byte (bits 15:8) into x8.
answer: srli x8, x5, 8 shifts the field down to the low byte, giving 0x00123456. Then addi x10, x0, 0xFF and x8, x8, x10 masks off everything above bit 7, leaving 0x00000056.
explain: General recipe: shift the field down to bit 0, then AND with a mask of that many ones.

q: Which shift instruction should you use to divide a signed negative number by 2?
explain: srai is the arithmetic right shift: it copies the sign bit. srli zero-fills and turns a negative into a large positive.

q: After xor x5, x5, x6 / xor x6, x5, x6 / xor x5, x5, x6, what has happened?
choices: x5 and x6 have been swapped
x5 holds the AND of the originals
explain: The XOR swap works because A⊕A = 0 and A⊕0 = A, so no temporary register is needed.

q: Which register holds the return address after jal?
explain: jal writes PC+4 into rd, and the convention is x1 (ra). Return with jalr x0, 0(x1).

q: Where does a function place its first return value?
explain: a0 (x10) carries both the first argument and the first return value; a1 (x11) carries a second return value.

q: A leaf procedure must save the return address on the stack before doing anything else.
explain: A leaf calls no other function, so nothing overwrites ra. It is the non-leaf that must save ra before any jal.

q: How do you allocate a 16-byte stack frame in RISC-V?
explain: The stack grows downward, so allocating means subtracting. Free it with addi sp, sp, 16 before returning.

q: List five reasons the stack is needed.
answer: 1) Preserving the return address, since nested jal calls overwrite ra. 2) Preserving callee-saved registers (s0–s11) so the caller's values survive. 3) Passing extra arguments beyond the eight that fit in a0–a7. 4) Holding local variables such as arrays and structs that do not fit in registers. 5) Supporting recursion, since each call needs its own independent frame.
explain: All five come down to registers being few and shared.

q: The 32-bit value 0x12345678 is stored at address 0x1000 on RISC-V. What byte is at 0x1000?
explain: RISC-V is little endian: the least significant byte goes at the lowest address.

q: Which memory segment grows upward and is managed by the programmer?
explain: The heap grows upward via allocation calls; the stack grows downward from high addresses.

q: Register x5 holds 0xFFFFFFFF and x6 holds 0x00000001. Does blt x5, x6, L branch? Does bltu x5, x6, L?
answer: blt branches: as signed values 0xFFFFFFFF is −1, and −1 < 1 is true. bltu does not branch: as unsigned, 0xFFFFFFFF is 4,294,967,295, which is not less than 1. The bits are identical; the instruction chooses the interpretation.
explain: This is the classic signed vs. unsigned comparison trap.

q: A B-type branch sits at PC = 0x100 and targets 0xD0. What immediate value is encoded?
explain: Byte offset = 0xD0 − 0x100 = −48. The immediate counts half-words, so −48 / 2 = −24.

q: The immediate in a B-type branch is the offset in bytes.
explain: It encodes half-words. The hardware computes target = PC + imm × 2, which doubles the reachable range since instruction addresses are always even.

q: For while (i < 10) { body; } with i in x11 and 10 in x12, which branch belongs at the top of the loop?
explain: The exit branch tests the inverted condition: leave when i >= 10.

q: Explain why lui x6, 0x12340 followed by addi x6, x6, 0x800 does not produce 0x12340800, and give the fix.
answer: addi sign-extends its 12-bit immediate. Since 0x800 has bit 11 set, it is treated as −2048, so the result is 0x12340000 − 0x800 = 0x1233F800. The fix is to add 1 to the upper 20 bits: lui x6, 0x12341, then addi x6, x6, 0x800 gives 0x12341000 − 0x800 = 0x12340800.
explain: Rule: if the lower 12 bits are ≥ 0x800, increment the value used in lui.

q: Why is jalr, not jal, used to return from a procedure?
choices: The return target is only known at run time and sits in ra, and jalr jumps to a computed address
explain: jal takes a fixed PC-relative label; a function can be called from anywhere, so the return address must come from a register.

q: Which is NOT true of a basic block?
choices: It has no branch inside it except possibly at the end
It has no branch target label inside it except possibly at the start
Compilers use it as an optimization unit
explain: A loop requires a backward branch and a target label, which would split the sequence into multiple basic blocks.

q: A processor has a 250 ps clock period. What is its clock rate?
explain: Rate = 1 / period = 1 / 250×10⁻¹² = 4×10⁹ = 4 GHz.

q: What is 2¹⁶?
explain: 2¹⁶ = 65,536, which is also the count of distinct 16-bit values.

q: How many characters does 7-bit ASCII encode?
explain: 2⁷ = 128 characters (0–127). Extended ASCII and Latin-1 use 8 bits for 256.

q: A higher clock rate always means better performance.
explain: CPU time = IC × CPI × cycle time. A machine with a faster clock but a much higher CPI or instruction count can still lose.
